topic: The 1943 Disappearance of the Hawaii Clipper
title: The One-Minute Radio Pause Before a 1938 Vanishing
description:
On July 29, 1938, the Pan American Airways flying boat Hawaii Clipper sent a routine position report over the Philippine Sea, followed eleven minutes later by a polite request from Flight Radio Officer William McGarty to stand by one minute due to rain static. No further word was ever heard from Captain Leo Terletzky or the fourteen other men aboard.

In this documentary, we examine the surviving Panay radio logs, the chemical laboratory tests on the USAT Meigs oil slick, and the Civil Aeronautics Authority report into the disappearance of the Martin M-130 aircraft NC14714 between Guam and Manila.

scenes.narration: A routine one-minute radio pause silenced a sixteen-ton flying boat forever.
scenes.query: Dramatic cinematic wide shot of a huge 1930s four-engine silver flying boat flying between dark tropical storm cloud layers over a dark ocean, lightning glow in the clouds, moody lighting, no text

scenes.narration: On July 29, 1938, Panay ground logs recorded the Hawaii Clipper asking to stand by one minute for rain static over the Philippine Sea.
scenes.query: Martin M-130 Hawaii Clipper flying boat

scenes.narration: That pause was never broken, and zero wreckage ever surfaced.
How does a routine complaint about static erase an airliner in sixty seconds?
scenes.query: Close-up of a 1930s brass Morse telegraph key and vintage radio headphones inside a dimly lit aircraft radio booth, rain streaking the small round window, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: Look closely at the Panay Island radio log at 12:11 PM Manila time, when the ground operator began sending routine Alameda weather updates to thirty-three-year-old Flight Radio Officer William McGarty.
scenes.query: Over-the-shoulder view of a 1930s flight radio operator in uniform headphones tapping a brass Morse code key in a cramped aluminum aircraft cabin, warm vacuum tube glow, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: Just eleven minutes earlier, at 12:00 PM sharp, the crew had transmitted a calm hourly position report from 9,100 feet: rough air, rain, 55 degrees Fahrenheit, and a nineteen-knot wind, while flying on instruments half the time between cloud layers.
scenes.query: Martin M-130 cockpit Pan American Airways

scenes.narration: Combined with McGarty's polite operational hold rather than an SOS, that noon report rules out a sudden cabin fire or flight-deck panic at 12:11 PM.
Before we go further, a quick historical note: while some files mislabel this case under 1943, that was the year its sister ship, the Philippine Clipper, crashed near Ukiah, California.

The Hawaii Clipper, registered as NC14714, vanished five years earlier, when it was the afternoon of July 29, 1938, in Manila, and still the evening of July 28 across the International Date Line in the mainland United States.
At 12:00 PM Manila time—04:00 Greenwich Mean Time—the flying boat fixed its position at Latitude 12 degrees 27 minutes North, Longitude 130 degrees 40 minutes East.
That placed the aircraft roughly 565 miles east of the Philippine coast, cruising westward against a wind from 247 degrees.
Eleven minutes later, when the Panay ground operator called with routine weather information for Alameda, McGarty broke in mid-transmission.
scenes.query: 1930s tropical radio station interior in the Philippines, back of an operator sitting before large black metal radio receivers with glowing dials, ceiling fan overhead, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: Press accounts often misspelled his name as McCarty, but William McGarty was a seasoned communicator who knew the exact sound of charged water droplets striking an aircraft antenna.
He tapped out eight words: stand by one minute, having trouble with rain static.
scenes.query: Extreme close-up of a gloved hand resting on a 1930s telegraph key, faint blue static electricity reflection on the metal casing, moody cinematic lighting, no text

scenes.narration: Sixty seconds passed at the Panay station.
From 12:12 PM to 12:15 PM, ground operators called the Hawaii Clipper repeatedly, only to be met by total radio silence.
scenes.query: Two 1930s radio operators in white shirts seen from behind in a humid Philippine radio room, leaning toward a silent loudspeaker, rainy window in background, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: Yet when the scheduled Manila arrival window between 2:30 PM and 3:30 PM came and went without a word, Pan American Airways executives were surprisingly calm.
Why did airline officials tell reporters at 6:30 PM that they were still not alarmed by six hours of dead air?
The airline's confidence rested on two concrete numbers listed in the Guam departure manifest from earlier that morning.

When the Hawaii Clipper lifted off from Apra Harbor at 6:08 AM Guam time—twenty-nine minutes behind schedule—it carried 1,138 pounds of mail and cargo, plus enough fuel and oil for 17.5 hours of flight.
scenes.query: Hawaii Clipper Pan Am water takeoff

scenes.narration: Because the 1,589-mile leg from Guam to Manila required an estimated 12.5 hours, the crew held five full hours of reserve fuel in their tanks.
Even more reassuring to Pan Am was the design of the Martin M-130 itself, which had first flown in Baltimore, Maryland, on December 30, 1934.
Built with a boat hull and wide waterline sea-wing sponsons for stability, the aircraft could theoretically set down on the open Pacific like a ship and ride out a storm.
If a lightning bolt or heavy rain had snapped the trailing wire antenna, Captain Leonard Terletzky had both the fuel and the hull to detour around bad weather.
scenes.query: Silhouette of two 1930s airline pilots in peaked caps inside a multi-engine flying boat cockpit, looking out through rain-lashed windshields at dark clouds, green instrument glow, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: At forty-three, Leo Terletzky was a veteran aviator with more than 9,200 total flight hours, including 1,626 hours over the Pacific.
Sitting beside him was twenty-six-year-old First Officer Mark Anderson Walker, who already held 1,900 flight hours—1,575 of them transpacific.
Walker and thirty-five-year-old Engineer Officer Howard L. Cox had just returned from Seattle, where they helped Boeing design the cockpit and engineering layout for the upcoming Boeing 314 Clipper.

In fact, out of the nine crewmen aboard Trip 229, five were licensed transport pilots: Terletzky, Walker, Second Officer George M. Davis, thirty-five-year-old Third Officer Jose M. Sauceda, and Fourth Officer John W. Jewett.
scenes.query: Wide shot of a 1930s flying boat flight deck from behind the crew, showing navigators and engineers working at brass instruments and control quadrants, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: Rounding out the nine-man crew were twenty-nine-year-old Assistant Engineer Officer Thomas B. Tatum, forty-year-old Flight Steward Ivan Parker, and Radio Officer McGarty.
Yet for all its luxury, the Hawaii Clipper carried an eerie historical shadow across the Pacific.

When this exact aircraft inaugurated the first revenue-generating transpacific passenger flight from Alameda to Manila on October 21, 1936, its cockpit was manned by Chief Pilot Edwin Musick and navigator Fred Noonan.
scenes.query: Edwin Musick Fred Noonan Pan Am

scenes.narration: Within twenty-one months of that triumph, Noonan vanished with Amelia Earhart in July 1937, and Musick died when the Sikorsky S-42B Samoan Clipper exploded in mid-air in January 1938.
Now, as darkness fell over Manila on July 29 and the 17.5-hour fuel limit ticked toward exhaustion, the third piece of that 1936 triumph was missing.
Just before midnight, an American Army transport ship arrived at the Clipper's last known coordinates—and what it found the next afternoon seemed to settle the mystery on the spot.
scenes.query: 1930s US Army freight transport ship at night on dark ocean waters, bright searchlight beams cutting through the mist and illuminating small flares on the water, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: When McGarty sent his final message at 12:11 PM, the 431-foot U.S. Army freight transport USAT Meigs was steaming roughly 87 to 100 miles west-northwest of the Clipper.
Diverted from its Manila-to-Honolulu voyage, the Meigs reached the last reported coordinates around midnight and searched the dark swells with spotlights and flares.
At dawn on July 30, six U.S. Army Martin B-10 bombers and two amphibians launched from Legaspi on Luzon, joining U.S. Navy warships and the minesweeper USS Penguin out of Guam.
The weather had cleared completely, leaving calm seas and crystalline visibility as the aircraft swept a 72,000-square-mile grid.
Then, at 5:10 PM Manila time on July 30, lookouts aboard the USAT Meigs spotted something at Latitude 12 degrees 06 minutes North, Longitude 130 degrees 20 minutes East.
scenes.query: View from the bridge wing of a 1930s steel cargo ship looking down at a calm ocean surface with a wide rainbow-colored circular oil slick glinting in afternoon sunlight, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: Located roughly twenty-eight nautical miles south-southeast of the Clipper's noon position, a circular oil slick between 500 and 1,500 feet in diameter lay across the water, smelling of petroleum vapors.
Before choppy overnight seas dissipated the slick, the crew of the Meigs lowered small boats and skimmed the surface for samples.
scenes.query: Sailors in 1930s work uniforms in a small wooden lifeboat on calm ocean swells, leaning over the gunwale to scoop seawater into small glass bottles, distant freighter in background, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: Newspaper headlines treated the slick as the Hawaii Clipper's watery grave, yet not a single seat cushion, mail sack, or wooden fitting was floating inside that circle.
Even more surprising was the actual size of the physical evidence delivered to government and Pan Am chemists.
scenes.query: 1930s chemistry laboratory bench with two tiny glass vials containing water and a thin dark film of oil, brass microscope and glass pipettes nearby, moody lighting, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: The two vials recovered by the Meigs contained less than three cubic centimeters of actual oil—roughly half a teaspoon in total.
To test those minuscule drops, chemists mixed genuine Clipper engine oil—of which the plane carried 120 gallons—with Pacific seawater for microscopic and chemical comparison.
scenes.query: Close-up of a 1930s chemist's hands holding two glass test tubes up to a warm lamp light, comparing dark heavy oil with lighter aviation oil, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: The laboratory verdict was unequivocal: the sample was heavy marine bunker fuel and ship or submarine lubricating oil, not high-octane aviation gasoline or aviation engine oil.

Some modern researchers, including those with The Lost Clipper project, have questioned whether 1938 testing on seawater-degraded traces could truly rule out a link so close to the last known position.
Officially, however, the three-man Civil Aeronautics Authority Air Safety Board panel—Robert D. Hoyt, Phil C. Salzman, and W. T. Miller—dismissed the slick in their November 18, 1938 report.
Instead, that same federal report highlighted a completely different clue recorded three hours after McGarty's radio went dead, hundreds of miles to the west.
According to testimony documented by the Civil Aeronautics Authority, a trusted employee of a telephone company was working on Lahuy Island in Camarines Sur, Philippines, on the afternoon of July 29.
Around 3:00 PM local time—nearly three hours after the 12:11 PM radio cutoff—he heard the unmistakable drone of a heavy multi-engine aircraft flying westward above the overcast.
scenes.query: 1930s Filipino lineman standing beside a wooden telephone pole on a lush tropical island hill, looking up at a thick gray blanket of unbroken clouds over the jungle, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: Military authorities checked flight logs across the region and verified that no other military or civilian aircraft were operating near Lahuy Island that afternoon.
On August 2, 1938, the sister ship China Clipper retraced the exact Guam-to-Manila flight path while search planes swept the jungles of Lahuy Island, finding nothing.
Still, when the CAA Air Safety Board published its findings in November, the investigators wrote that the Lahuy Island acoustic sighting cannot be ignored.
Why would the Hawaii Clipper fly for three hours in complete radio silence, passing directly along its intended route toward Manila without ever attempting to land?
scenes.query: Distant silhouette of a four-engine 1930s flying boat skimming above the tops of gray storm clouds in late afternoon light, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: In the Winter 2023 issue of the American Aviation Historical Society Journal, engineer and aviation historian J.B. Rivard connected that 3:00 PM sound directly back to McGarty's final words.
In Rivard's technical reanalysis, the severe rain static reported at 12:11 PM was the immediate electrostatic precursor to a direct lightning strike on the aircraft.
scenes.query: Dramatic cinematic shot of a blinding bolt of lightning striking the nose and tail antenna of a 1930s silver flying boat inside a dark rain cloud, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: A massive electrical transient would have instantly burned out the radio equipment and damaged flight instruments or control cables, while blinding or incapacitating the pilots at the controls.
scenes.query: Darkened 1930s aircraft cockpit with shattered or smoked glass instrument dials and a faint wisp of electrical smoke near the radio panel, moody blue storm light outside, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: Because five of the nine crew members were qualified pilots, reserve officers could have taken the controls and kept the crippled flying boat airborne on a westward heading.

Flying blind between cloud layers without radios or working navigation aids, the plane would have reached the Philippine coast near Lahuy Island around 3:00 PM before crashing into dense mountain jungle or coastal waters.
That compares favorably against the second major hypothesis from 1938: a sudden mid-air fuel vapor explosion or structural failure of the waterline sea-wing sponsons in rough air.
While a catastrophic breakup at 9,100 feet explains the abrupt silence, high-velocity water impacts invariably leave floating debris—and the Meigs and B-10 bombers found none.

What I keep coming back to is the timing of that Lahuy Island report. A lightning strike at 12:11 PM is the only single mechanism that accounts for McGarty's rain static message, a dead radio, zero floating debris in the open sea, and heavy engines passing the Philippine coast three hours later.
scenes.query: Archivist's desk in a dimly lit room, hands holding a magnifying glass over vintage 1930s photographs of a four-engine flying boat, warm desk lamp glow, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: Yet despite aerial searches and a monetary reward offered by Pan Am, no wreckage was ever found on Luzon—which led later writers to look closely at who was sitting in the passenger cabin.
scenes.query: Interior of a luxurious 1930s flying boat passenger lounge, plush upholstered seats, round windows showing dark rain outside, silhouettes of suited men talking quietly, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: When Trip 229 originally departed San Francisco Bay from Alameda around 3:00 PM on July 23, 1938, it carried twelve passengers alongside its nine-man crew.
Six of those passengers disembarked when the flying boat landed at Pearl Harbor in Honolulu around 8:00 AM on July 24.
Only six men remained aboard for the island-hopping overnight stops across Midway Atoll, Wake Island, and Guam.
Two of them were prominent scientists conducting an active experiment right outside the cabin windows: Dr. Fred C. Meier and Dr. Earl Baldwin McKinley.
Meier, a senior plant pathologist for the U.S. Department of Agriculture who coined the term aerobiology, had persuaded Charles Lindbergh and Pan Am to let him trap high-altitude microbes.
scenes.query: 1930s scientist in a suit inside an aircraft cabin holding a small brass and glass slide holder near an aerodynamic port, soft daylight, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: Working with McKinley—a U.S. Army Reserve Colonel and Dean of the School of Medicine at George Washington University—Meier used sticky glass microscope slides exposed to the slipstream to study transoceanic disease and fungal spores.

Two other passengers were aviation figures: Major Howard C. French of the U.S. Army Air Corps Reserve, former head of the Oregon Aeronautics Board, and Kenneth A. Kennedy, Pan Am's Pacific Division Traffic Manager.
It was the final pair of passengers, however, who sparked decades of espionage theories.
scenes.query: Two men in 1930s fedora hats and trench coats walking toward a flying boat dock at dawn in Guam, carrying leather briefcases, seen from behind, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: Edward E. Wyman, a former U.S. Navy Lieutenant Commander and Vice President of the Curtiss-Wright Export Corporation, was traveling to China to negotiate fighter aircraft and engine sales to the Nationalist Chinese government.
Beside him was Wah Sun Choy—known as Watson Choy—a Jersey City, New Jersey restaurateur and President of the Chinese War Relief Committee.
Choy was traveling to deliver war relief funds raised by Chinese-Americans to Chiang Kai-shek's government during its war with Imperial Japan.

Secondary websites and conspiracy books widely claim Choy carried three million dollars in U.S. currency or gold certificates inside his briefcase, though other historians dispute that figure as a massive postwar exaggeration unsupported by any 1938 customs manifest or insurance claim.
scenes.query: Close-up of a locked 1930s brown leather briefcase resting beside a passenger seat inside a vintage airliner cabin, dim lighting, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: Even so, could the presence of Wyman and Choy have made the Hawaii Clipper a target for foreign interception in the summer of 1938?

Beginning with journalist Ronald W. Jackson's 1980 book China Clipper and expanded in Charles N. Hill's 2000 book Fix on the Rising Sun, researchers proposed a third theory: a mid-ocean hijacking by Imperial Japanese agents.

Under this hypothesis, intelligence operatives stowed away at Guam or nearby Rota or Saipan waters, overpowered the crew after takeoff, cut off the radio, and diverted the plane to Japanese-controlled Mandate territory such as Tinian or Dublon Island in Truk Lagoon.
Proponents argue that Japan wanted to block Wyman's fighter plane deal, seize Choy's relief funds, and reverse-engineer the Martin M-130 airframe and its Pratt and Whitney Twin Wasp engines.

They also point to the Japanese Navy cargo ship Canberra Maru, which conducted a final search check near Douglas Reef—Okino Tori-shima—on August 7 before all search efforts ended on August 10, allegedly sending cryptic radio traffic.

In a strange twist of history, both the USAT Meigs and the Canberra Maru were later sunk by enemy dive-bombers in 1942 during World War II—the Meigs at Darwin, Australia, and the Canberra Maru during the Battle of Guadalcanal.

Nor did the Martin M-130 fleet survive the war: after the Philippine Clipper crashed in 1943, the China Clipper crashed on landing in Port of Spain, Trinidad, in 1945, meaning all three $417,000 sister ships met violent ends.
Yet when we test the Japanese hijacking claim against hard evidence, the theory falls apart.
Not a single document mentioning the Hawaii Clipper has ever surfaced in post-World War II Japanese military archives.

When investigator Guy Noffsinger and The Lost Clipper project conducted ground-penetrating radar expeditions in Micronesia searching for alleged burials under concrete on Dublon Island, they found no human remains or aircraft parts.
scenes.query: Modern researchers pushing a wheeled ground-penetrating radar unit across an overgrown concrete slab in a tropical Pacific jungle, seen from behind, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: Even a mysterious flying boat wreck photographed in Truk Lagoon in 1964—long cited as proof of the capture—was definitively identified as a post-World War II British Short Sunderland.

Meanwhile, the 1938 CAA Air Safety Board report confirmed the Hawaii Clipper had 4,806 airframe hours, was structurally airworthy, and left zero physical evidence behind, forcing the board to declare the cause undetermined.

If you ask me, the espionage theory invents a complex plot to solve a tragedy that meteorology and physics already explain. When William McGarty tapped out his warning about rain static at 9,100 feet, he was unintentionally diagnosing the electrical hazard that silenced his radio—and whether the Clipper fell into the Philippine Sea or flew crippled over Lahuy Island, the storm claimed it.
scenes.query: Wide atmospheric view of the empty Philippine Sea at twilight under towering tropical rain clouds, a single shaft of sunlight hitting the dark water, no text, no faces

scenes.narration: More than eight decades later, sixteen tons of aluminum and fifteen men remain missing behind a one-minute pause that never ended.

If this case stays with you, there is another file from four years earlier where twenty-year-old artist Everett Ruess vanished into the canyons of Escalante, Utah, leaving his two burros penned in a Davis Gulch corral and the Latin word NEMO 1934 chiseled into the sandstone.

watch_next.summary:
In November 1934, 20-year-old artist Everett Ruess walked into the canyons of Escalante, Utah, and vanished without a trace. Months later, searchers in Davis Gulch found his two burros penned inside a makeshift brush corral, an undated final letter to his brother Waldo, and the Latin word NEMO 1934 chiseled into the sandstone.

This documentary investigates the disappearance of Everett Ruess through the physical evidence left behind in the Grand Staircase-Escalante backcountry, examining the timeline paradox of the Davis Gulch corral, his final messages, and the 2009 Comb Ridge DNA controversy
